analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set an enforceable legal limit for PFAS chemicals in drinking water within two years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 8 cosponsors from both parties, sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to do within two years what it had never done: set an enforceable national limit on perfluorinated chemicals — including PFOS and PFOA, often called "forever chemicals" — in public drinking water. Today there is no such federal limit, so water systems are not legally required to test for or remove these chemicals, which the Congressional Research Service notes accumulate in human blood. The bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water contaminated with perfluorinated compounds, especially those living near military bases, airports, and industrial sites where PFOS and PFOA were used or dumped. An enforceable EPA drinking water regulation would legally require water systems to test for these chemicals and treat the water when levels exceed the limit, turning an unregulated exposure into a monitored, enforceable one. The bill text names PFOS and PFOA specifically, the two most notorious of these chemicals, which the CRS summary says are manufactured compounds used in consumer products that accumulate in human blood.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA, within two years of enactment, to publish a maximum contaminant level goal and issue a national primary drinking water regulation covering perfluorinated compounds, explicitly including PFOS and PFOA — creating a legally binding federal limit where none exists.

Once a national primary drinking water regulation is in place, public water systems must test for the chemical and take action when it exceeds the legal limit, so exposure that is currently invisible to consumers becomes measured and enforceable.

Addresses chemicals that accumulate in human blood, according to the Congressional Research Service, meaning a drinking water limit reduces ongoing body burden for everyone on a public water system, not just people who can afford bottled water or home filtration.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the direct compliance costs would fall on public water systems, which would have to test for the chemicals and install treatment when levels exceed the new limit — costs that would be passed on to ratepayers, with smaller systems facing the steepest per-household burden. The EPA would bear the cost of the rulemaking itself. Chemical manufacturers would face tighter regulation and greater legal exposure as enforceable limits make contamination easier to prove.
analysis.who_pays_short: Water utilities, ratepayers, and chemical makers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: water systems would have to test for the chemicals and, where levels exceed the new limit, install treatment such as carbon filtration, and those costs would flow to ratepayers — hitting customers of small water systems hardest, since fixed costs are spread over fewer households.

The two-year deadline is aggressive. Setting a drinking water standard normally involves years of health and treatment-technology review, so a hard statutory deadline risks a rushed standard, legal challenge, or both — a fair objection even from supporters, though Congress has imposed similar statutory deadlines under the Safe Drinking Water Act before.
The bill sets the limit but provides no federal money to help utilities pay for testing and treatment, leaving the entire compliance bill with water systems and their customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a legally enforceable limit on chemicals that accumulate in human blood and were entirely unregulated in drinking water — is large for the millions of people on contaminated water systems, and the costs, while real, are the ordinary price of safe drinking water that utilities already bear for dozens of other contaminants. The main design weakness is the tight two-year deadline and the absence of funding assistance for utilities, especially small ones. The honest bottom line is that these tradeoffs were never debated at all: the bill never even got a hearing or a mark-up, so no version of this cost-benefit question was ever put to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee's Environment Subcommittee in the summer of 2017, nothing ever came of it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced the bill on June 29, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Environment, which is where a bill typically goes to be debated, amended, or ignored.
No hearing, mark-up, or vote ever followed. The bill's final recorded action was the sponsor's introductory remarks on July 14, 2017, two weeks after introduction.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, roughly 18 months later, and every unpassed bill from that Congress expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that make perfluorinated chemicals avoided an enforceable federal drinking water limit and the liability that comes with one, and water systems avoided testing and treatment costs. Communities with contaminated water gained nothing: no federal standard existed when the bill was introduced, and none existed when it died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS makers; water utilities without new costs

sides.party_line_note: Support was clearly bipartisan — 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans cosponsored — but because the bill never reached a vote, no one's opposition, or anyone's final position, was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have given these chemicals an enforceable federal drinking water limit for the first time, which raises cleanup obligations and makes contamination cases easier to prove in court. A limit that never arrived meant no new federal exposure, and drinking water contamination stayed legally unaddressed.

Utilities would have had to test for perfluorinated compounds and install treatment where levels exceeded the new limit, with costs passed to ratepayers. Their interest in avoiding compliance costs pulls against the public's interest in safe water, though the communities they serve are the same people the standard protects.

A national drinking water regulation would have created nationwide demand for testing and treatment technology, such as carbon filtration, to remove the chemicals. Their business grows only if the public actually gets cleaner water.
